newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Tennis-Chang slain by Spanish giant-killer.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Tennis-Chang slain by Spanish giant-killer.

text.p: Carlos Moya's giant-killing run at the Australian Open reached new heights on Thursday when he overwhelmed world number two Michael Chang in straight sets to reach his first grand slam final.
The unseeded Spaniard, ranked 25 in the world, surpassed his sensational first round victory over defending champion Boris Becker to brush aside Chang 7-5 6-2 6-4 in just over two hours.
"Today I did something big, I played in an unbelievable way," Moya told reporters after his emphatic victory.
In only his fourth grand slam tournament, tournament heart-throb Moya has revelled in the slow hardcourt conditions and the extreme summer temperatures.
On Thursday, he established his dominance on the baseline, neutralising Chang's challenge with successive forehand winners.
As his grip on the match tightened, the Spaniard came in to the net, distracting a surprisingly nervous Chang whose usually reliable baseline game was littered with errors.
"I knew before the match that I had to take risks to beat him, if you stay on the baseline against him you lose," said Moya, who has won just two tour titles, both on clay.
Chang made a third-set challenge, building up a 3-1 and 40-15 lead on his serve, but Moya managed to step up his game.
"I kept going and broke him back and that was one of the keys. That was the only point he was leading," Moya said.
Chang showed rare moments of emotion and stared repeatedly at his racquet as the confident Moya headed to victory.
"To be honest I don't think I was quite as sharp as I have been, I made a few more errors today and it hurt me," said Chang, a beaten finalist in Melbourne last year.
The stocky American consistently drove the ball either long or into the top of the net and missed several simple smash volleys that he would normally drive home.
The Barcelona-based Moya raised his arms in triumph and saluted the crowd's standing ovation after sealing the victory with his second match point.

The 20-year-old underdog, his long brown hair held back by a bandana, has captured the hearts of Melbourne's teenage girls and the imagination of a sport-loving public hoping to see the birth of a new hero.
On Thursday, Moya did not let either party down, crushing Chang to silence those who once rated him a mere clay court specialist unable to adapt to other surfaces.
Moya, who did not advance beyond the second round in last year's four major tournaments, exposed Chang's weak serve, breaking the American on eight occasions.
Although he has not won a grand slam title since lifting the French Open as a 17-year-old in 1989, Chang had played the most consistent tennis of any major name in Melbourne.
But the tall, languid Spaniard seemed unimpressed with his opponent's reputation.

Moya becomes the first Spanish man to reach the finals of the Australian Open since Andres Gimeno lost to the great Rod Laver in 1969. He will meet either world number one Pete Sampras or fifth-seeded Austrian Thomas Muster in Sunday's final.
Moya said he did not care whom he would play and promised to watch Sampras play on Friday from the comfort of his bed.
"He's number one, but I have beaten number two and number six," he said.
"I am not going to go onto the court a loser. There were 128 players the first day, now we are only two, anything can happen."
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
